name: Vishalakshi Temple, Varanasi
deity: Devi as Vishalakshi (Vishalakshmi), the Wide-Eyed Goddess, with Kala Bhairava as her guardian
period: Ancient Devi seat of Kashi, one of the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas; the present temple was completed in 1893
dynasty: Nagarathar (Nattukottai Chettiar) merchant patrons of Tamil Nadu
style: North Indian haveli-style shrine with a small Dravidian gopuram
summary: Vishalakshi is the wide-eyed Mother of Kashi, named in the Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha stotram as "Varanasyam Vishalakshi", where tradition says Sati's earring or eye fell near Manikarnika; her temple at Mir Ghat was rebuilt by Tamil Nagarathar devotees.

sections.history: Kashi is the city of Shiva, yet its tradition holds that the Mother is never absent from it, and Vishalakshi is her seat here. The Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha stotram, attributed to Adi Shankara, names the goddess of this city in the line "Varanasyam Vishalakshi", which places the shrine among the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas. The Kashi Khanda of the Skanda Purana praises her greatness and counts her among the Nava Gauri, the nine goddesses of the city's own pilgrimage. The present temple at Mir Ghat was completed in 1893, rebuilt and maintained since the nineteenth century by the Nagarathar community of Tamil Nadu, whose devotion to Kashi has long linked the far south with the banks of the Ganga.
sections.architecture: The temple lies in the lanes above Mir Ghat, close to the old Dharmakupa well and a short walk from Manikarnika, and it is reached through a narrow passage rather than a grand forecourt. Its form recalls a Varanasi haveli, with an enclosed court and a compact sanctum, yet the hand of its southern patrons shows in a modest Dravidian gopuram and in Tamil inscriptions. The sanctum is said to hold two images of the goddess in dark stone: the older Adi Vishalakshi, and a larger image, dressed in jewels and flowers, set up when Tamil devotees renovated the shrine.
sections.legends: The pilgrim's story begins with Sati, who gave up her life at her father Daksha's sacrifice. Shiva, in grief, carried her body across the land, and as it was divided, every place where a part fell became a seat of the Mother. In Kashi tradition says it was the jewel of her ear-ornament that fell beside Manikarnika, which gave the ghat its name; another account holds that it was her eye, and the name Vishalakshi, the wide-eyed, is read in that light. Kashi has a second tale, told in the Skanda Purana. The sage Vyasa, finding that no household in the city offered him food, spoke a curse against it, and the goddess came to him as a housewife and fed him. Devotees remember here a Mother who nourishes the hungry.
sections.festivals: Kajali Teej, kept in the dark fortnight of Bhadrapada (August to September), is regarded as the temple's principal festival, when women gather to sing and pray for the well-being of their families. Chaitra Navratri (March or April) and Sharad Navratri (September or October) are observed for nine days in honour of the goddess in her many forms, and the temple is one of the stations of Kashi's Nava Gauri pilgrimage. Dates follow the Hindu lunar calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Reach Vishalakshi on foot, as Kashi intends, by threading the old lanes toward the river and leaving the bustle of the ghats for the shrine's enclosed court. Pause at the threshold, then come before the goddess for darshan. Many pilgrims pair the visit with a walk to nearby Manikarnika and a prayer at Kashi Vishwanath, so that the Mother and the Lord of Kashi are honoured together. The southern inscriptions and the gopuram are a gentle reminder of how far the devotion of this shrine has travelled to reach the Ganga.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning, around 5:00 to 6:00, until late evening, around 9:00 to 10:00, though listed hours vary; confirm timings locally, especially during Navratri.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is recommended: sarees, salwar kameez, or kurta with trousers or dhoti, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside, and it is wise to carry little in the crowded lanes.
visit.photography: Photography rules are set by the temple and may change. It is customary not to photograph the sanctum or the image of the goddess, so ask the temple staff before using a camera or phone.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is at Mir Ghat in the old city, near Manikarnika Ghat and the Kashi Vishwanath area. Varanasi Junction railway station is about 4.5 km away and Lal Bahadur Shastri International Airport about 25 km. Vehicles cannot easily enter the lanes near the ghats, so take an auto or cycle rickshaw as far as the road allows and walk the last stretch.
